content: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent psychiatric condition that affects children and adolescents. Amphetamines are among the most frequently prescribed medications for managing ADHD symptoms. There are three primary types of amphetamines used in treatment: dexamphetamine, lisdexamphetamine, and mixed amphetamine salts. These can be further categorized into short-acting and long-acting formulations. Despite their widespread use, a systematic review evaluating the efficacy and safety of amphetamines in this population had not been conducted prior to this study. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of amphetamines in children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in August 2015 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, ProQuest Dissertation and Theses, and the Networked Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov, and reference lists of relevant studies and reviews were examined. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with either parallel-group or cross-over designs. These trials compared amphetamine derivatives to placebo in pediatric populations under the age of 18 diagnosed with ADHD. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, focusing on participant characteristics, study settings, interventions, methodologies, and outcomes. For continuous outcomes, standardized mean differences (SMDs) were calculated, while risk ratios (RRs) were used for dichotomous outcomes. Meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model where possible, including an analysis of the most commonly reported adverse events. A total of 23 trials were included in the review, comprising 8 parallel-group and 15 cross-over trials, with a combined total of 2,675 participants aged 3 to 17 years. All studies compared amphetamines to placebo, with study durations ranging from 14 days to 365 days, though most lasted less than six months. The majority of the studies were conducted in the United States, with three studies conducted in Europe. Eleven studies were judged to have a high risk of bias due to issues such as inadequate blinding, failure to account for dropouts, and incomplete reporting of predefined outcomes. The remaining 12 studies were deemed to have an unclear risk of bias due to insufficient reporting. Amphetamines were found to reduce the severity of core ADHD symptoms based on parent ratings (SMD -0.57; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.86 to -0.27; 7 studies; 1,247 participants; very low-quality evidence), teacher ratings (SMD -0.55; 95% CI -0.83 to -0.27; 5 studies; 745 participants; low-quality evidence), and clinician ratings (SMD -0.84; 95% CI -1.32 to -0.36; 3 studies; 813 participants; very low-quality evidence). Additionally, a higher proportion of children were rated as responders on the Clinical Global Impression-Improvement (CGI-I) scale when taking amphetamines (RR 3.36; 95% CI 2.48 to 4.55; 9 studies; 2,207 participants; very low-quality evidence). However, amphetamines were associated with several adverse events. The most commonly reported side effects included decreased appetite, insomnia or difficulty sleeping, abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, headaches, and anxiety. Specifically, amphetamines were linked to a higher proportion of participants experiencing decreased appetite (RR 6.31; 95% CI 2.58 to 15.46; 11 studies; 2,467 participants), insomnia (RR 3.80; 95% CI 2.12 to 6.83; 10 studies; 2,429 participants), and abdominal pain (RR 1.44; 95% CI 1.03 to 2.00; 10 studies; 2,155 participants). Overall, children in the amphetamine group were more likely to experience at least one adverse event compared to those in the placebo group (RR 1.30; 95% CI 1.18 to 1.44; 6 studies; 1,742 participants; low-quality evidence). Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore differences based on amphetamine preparation (dexamphetamine, lisdexamphetamine, mixed amphetamine salts), release formulation (long-acting versus short-acting), and funding source (industry-funded versus non-industry-funded). Significant differences were observed in the proportion of participants experiencing decreased appetite across both amphetamine preparation (P < 0.00001) and release formulation subgroups (P = 0.008). Additionally, differences in retention rates were noted in the amphetamine release formulation subgroup (P = 0.03). The authors concluded that most of the included studies were at high risk of bias, and the overall quality of evidence was low to very low for most outcomes. While amphetamines appear to be effective in reducing core ADHD symptoms in the short term, they are associated with a range of adverse events. The review did not find evidence to support the superiority of one amphetamine derivative over another or to indicate differences between long-acting and short-acting formulations. Future research should focus on longer-term trials (exceeding 12 months), include more psychosocial outcomes such as quality of life and parental stress, and ensure transparent reporting of results.
